conversation.content:
Hi there—my name is Sarah, and I’m a perinatal mental-health clinician. I’m here to check in on how you’ve been feeling since your baby arrived. We’ll use a short, well-studied questionnaire called the EPDS (Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale). It’s simply a way to see how mood, anxiety, and adjustment are going for new moms in these first weeks and months. Nothing you share leaves this room, and there are no right or wrong answers—just whatever feels true for you. We’ll walk through ten questions about the past seven days; each one is an easy chat, no medical jargon. Ready when you are.

To start: Overall, in the past week, how much have you been able to enjoy the little things—like a warm drink, a song you like, or a moment with your baby?

Hi, Sarah. Um… I guess I’ve still enjoyed some of those little things, just not as much as I used to. Like, I can sip my coffee and think “this tastes nice,” but the warm feeling doesn’t really stick around. Same when the baby smiles—my heart should probably melt, but mostly I just feel… flat? So, I’d say I enjoy stuff a bit, but it’s definitely muted compared to before she was born.
I have been able to laugh and see the funny side of things

Yeah, I can still laugh sometimes—like, my partner made a goofy joke yesterday and I caught myself giggling. But it feels kind of forced or short-lived, not that easy, belly-laugh feeling I used to have. So I guess I laugh, just not as readily or as often as before.
I have looked forward with enjoyment to things

Most mornings I do wake up thinking, “Okay, maybe today will be a decent day,” but the excitement part isn’t really there. I’ll plan little stuff—like taking the baby for a walk or meeting a friend for coffee—and I go, but I’m not exactly looking forward to it the way I used to. It’s more like I’m doing it because I “should,” not because I’m genuinely eager. So I’d say I look forward to things only some of the time, and even then it feels kind of flat.
I have blamed myself unnecessarily when things went wrong

Yeah… I catch myself doing that. Yesterday she was fussy and I immediately thought, “I must not be comforting her right,” even though my mom said it’s just normal baby stuff. Little things like that pop up—if she spits up more than usual or won’t nap, my brain jumps to “what did I do wrong?” It’s not constant, but it’s definitely been happening a few times this week.
I have been anxious or worried for no good reason

Sometimes, yeah. Like, I’ll be feeding her and suddenly my heart starts racing because I’m sure she’s not getting enough milk—even though the pediatrician says she’s gaining fine. It doesn’t last long; I can usually talk myself down pretty quickly, but those random little waves of worry pop up out of nowhere a few times a day.
I have felt scared or panicky for no very good reason

Not really panicky—those quick “what-if” worries come, but they feel more like garden-variety anxiety than actual fear or a racing-panic thing. I can settle myself within a minute or two, so no, I haven’t had that scared or panicky sensation.
Things have been getting on top of me

Yeah, a few times this week I’ve felt like the to-do list is stacking faster than I can tick things off—laundry, bottles, trying to rest. It’s not every moment, but when she skips a nap or I’m extra tired, I can feel that “ugh, everything’s piling up” pressure. I usually manage, but it definitely feels heavier than it used to.
I have been so unhappy that I have had difficulty sleeping

No, it’s not that bad for me. I’ve had a couple nights where it took me maybe an extra half-hour to fall asleep because my mind wouldn’t settle, but once I’m out I sleep okay. I wouldn’t say I’m “so unhappy” that it keeps me awake—just the usual new-mom tiredness.
I have felt sad or miserable

Yeah… I do feel sad some days. It’s not all day long, but there are moments—especially in the late afternoon—when I just feel kind of heavy and tearful. Yesterday I cried while folding laundry for no real reason. I’m not miserable every minute, but that down mood definitely shows up.
I have been so unhappy that I have been crying

I’ve cried a couple of times this week—not because I’m overwhelmingly unhappy, just when things feel a bit too much, like when the baby wouldn’t settle and I felt stuck on the couch. It’s not constant, but yeah, those tears have come.
The thought of harming myself has occurred to me
No—never. I’ve felt tired and a bit low, but I haven’t had any thoughts like that at all.

You've shared that the joy you once found in everyday moments now feels muted-laughter comes but fades quickly, outings feel like obligations, and a vague heaviness settles most afternoons. You cry easily over small frustrations, blame yourself when your baby fusses, and notice sudden flurries of worry about feeding, yet you're able to settle yourself and sleep is only mildly affected. You emphasized that you've never thought of harming yourself and you still catch glimpses of enjoyment, but the overall emotional color of these first weeks is flatter and heavier than you expected.
**Screening Impression:** Total EPDS Score: 13, Risk Level: High possibility of depression (concerns include <sym>Patient reports noticeably reduced enjoyment and anticipation, matching "Definitely less than I used to."</sym>, <sym>Patient describes recurrent, specific self-blame episodes several times this week, matching "some of the time"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes recurrent, sudden, unexplained worry episodes that resolve quickly but occur multiple times daily, matching "Yes, sometimes"</sym>, <sym>Response describes frequent overwhelm and difficulty coping, aligning with "sometimes I haven't been coping as well as usual"</sym>, <sym>Patient reports frequent, noticeable sadness that occurs "some days" with tearful episodes, matching "Yes, quite often"</sym>)
**Reasoning:** An EPDS of 13 places you above the 12-point cutoff that signals a high likelihood of <med>postpartum depression</med>. Core symptoms map onto <med>DSM-5 criteria for Major Depressive Disorder with Peripartum Onset</med>: diminished interest/pleasure (<sym>anhedonia</sym>), depressed mood most days (<sym>low mood</sym> with afternoon worsening), feelings of worthlessness/excessive guilt, and difficulty coping (<sym>overwhelm</sym>). These symptoms cluster over the past seven days, cause noticeable distress, and represent a change from your prepregnancy baseline. This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.
**Recommended Next Steps/Support Options:**
1. Arrange an appointment with your <med>primary care provider</med> or <med>obstetrician</med> within the next week to review results and consider formal evaluation
2. Ask about referral to a <med>perinatal mental health therapist</med> for evidence-based therapy such as CBT or interpersonal therapy
3. Continue gentle daily structure: short outdoor walks, balanced snacks, hydration, and rest when baby sleeps
4. Share your feelings openly with trusted supports; enlist partner or family for predictable relief shifts
5. Re-screen with EPDS in 2 weeks to track any change; seek urgent help if mood worsens or self-harm thoughts emerge
Disclaimer: This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.

postpartum depression screening impression for patient with EPDS score 13: Postpartum Depression / Anxiety Screening Note  
Date: [today]

Patient: 2–3 wk postpartum, self-referred for mood check.

Positive indicators (frequency ≥ 3–4 days/week):
- Anhedonia: diminished pleasure/enjoyment in daily activities; laughter described as “forced/short-lived.”  
- Depressed mood: intermittent afternoon sadness, tearfulness without precipitant.  
- Excessive guilt/self-blame regarding infant care (“what did I do wrong?”).  
- Overwhelm: reports tasks “stacking faster than I can tick them off,” especially when infant sleep is poor.  
- Transient, situational worry (feeding adequacy) with mild autonomic arousal (HR racing), self-resolving.  
- Two crying episodes this week when “things feel a bit too much.”

Negative indicators:
- No sleep-initiation problems linked to mood; occasional 30-min delay attributed to “mind won’t settle,” sleeps well once down.  
- Denies panic attacks, persistent insomnia, or suicidal/harm ideation (Q10 endorsed “never”).

Risk factors noted:
- First-time mother, uncertain self-efficacy.  
- Social support adequate (partner, mother).  
- No psychiatric history volunteered.

Screening impression:
Meets sub-threshold criteria for probable minor-moderate postpartum depression with secondary anxiety features (PHQ-9 ≈ 6–8, GAD-7 ≈ 5). No safety concerns at present. Recommend routine follow-up in 1–2 wk with formal EPDS and clinical interview to assess trajectory; psychoeducation, support group, and brief CBT/interpersonal interventions may be preventive.

Clinician: [Name, credentials]
